findings.title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure
findings.body: FixedQueuePool builds each queue.Queue() with the default maxsize (unlimited), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always returns after put(). The class comment claims natural backpressure, but Arroyo will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing as fast as the broker allows. A single slow group blocks commits for its whole partition (offsets cannot advance past the oldest incomplete offset), while every later message on that partition is retained in memory. A hot or stuck subscription can therefore grow process memory without bound and turn the clog this PR is meant to avoid into an OOM, without ever pausing the consumer.

findings.title: Strategy close kills the shared worker pool and stops commits before drain
findings.body: The queue pool and its worker threads are created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and shared by every strategy from create_with_partitions. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets the commit-loop shutdown event, joins that thread, then calls FixedQueuePool.shutdown(). shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag before Queue.shutdown(), so a worker blocked in get() exits on ShutDown and does not drain remaining items, and a worker between iterations leaves the loop immediately. Offsets finished only during that drain are never committed because the commit thread is already stopped. On partition revoke/rebalance Arroyo closes this strategy and calls create_with_partitions again; the new strategy reuses the already-shut-down pool, so later messages are not processed for the rest of the process lifetime. join() also ignores its timeout and can block about 5s plus 5s per worker.

findings.title: Kafka commits are invoked from a background thread
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls commit_function (the Arroyo commit callback, which reaches the librdkafka consumer) every second. Every other strategy in this consumer commits from the processing thread. librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and that callback races with poll, submit, and close/terminate on the main thread. terminate() does not even join the commit thread, so a commit can run while the consumer is shutting down. This can crash the consumer, commit a torn offset map, or lose the in-flight commit.

findings.title: Failed messages are acked and never retried
findings.body: OrderedQueueWorker.complete_offset runs in a finally block, including after result_processor raises, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit also add+completes the offset when decode, grouping, or put fails. The strategy docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing, but any exception is logged and then treated as done, with no DLQ on the uptime-results consumer. A transient DB or downstream failure is therefore committed (offset+1) and will not be redelivered, so an uptime check that failed to be handled can be dropped permanently. The new error-handling test asserts the opposite (no commit) and only sleeps 0.2s while the commit loop waits 1s, so it neither matches the code nor reliably checks it.

findings.title: Queue-depth test races the workers and can flake
findings.body: test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. Workers are already running and the processor is a no-op, so the queues can be empty before that assertion. test_different_groups_distributed likewise requires 20 hashed keys to land in all 3 buckets, which is not guaranteed. Both can fail on a quiet CI run without a product bug.
